unit.title: Irony, Connotation & Reading Between the Lines
unit.subtitle: Sarcasmo, connotación, doble sentido and pragmatic implicature

grammar.title: When the meaning lives under the words
grammar.intro: Near-native comprehension is mostly about what is not said. Spanish loads attitude into tone (sarcasm), into word choice (connotation: delgado vs esquelético), and into context (implicature: “hace frío aquí” = shut the window). At C2 you decode the intended message, not the literal one — and you learn which near-synonym quietly reveals the speaker's stance.

sections.heading: Verbal irony and sarcasm
sections.body: Ironía verbal states the opposite of the intended meaning; sarcasmo is its biting form. Delivery is everything: “¡Qué bien, otra reunión!” said flatly means the exact reverse. Cues include a deadpan tone, an over-enthusiastic word against a tedious event, or markers like sí, claro and faltaría más read against context.

ex.en: —I'm an hour late. —How punctual you are!

ex.es: Sí, claro, seguro que esta vez sí llama.
ex.en: Yeah, right, I'm sure he'll call this time.

sections.heading: Denotation vs connotation
sections.body: Near-synonyms share a denotation (dictionary sense) but carry different connotation (attitude). Delgado is neutral, flaco plainer, esquelético negative. Curioso flatters; cotilla disparages. Ahorrador praises thrift; tacaño condemns stinginess. Choosing one over another silently reveals how the speaker feels.

ex.es: No es ahorrador, es tacaño: no invita ni a un café.
ex.en: He's not thrifty, he's stingy: he won't even buy you a coffee.

ex.es: Dijo que soy curioso, pero quería decir cotilla.
ex.en: He said I'm inquisitive, but he meant nosy.

sections.heading: Pragmatic implicature
sections.body: Speakers often mean more than they say, trusting you to infer it. “Hace frío aquí” is rarely weather talk — it's a request to shut the window. “¿Tú no tenías examen mañana?” hints you should be studying. This is implicatura: the literal words are a polite vehicle for the real, unstated point.
conj: = we should leave / you should go

ex.en: The phone's awfully quiet today, isn't it?
ex.note: implies: you were supposed to call someone

ex.es: Yo que tú, me lo pensaría dos veces.
ex.en: If I were you, I'd think twice.
ex.note: a veiled warning, not neutral advice

sections.heading: Understatement and double meaning
sections.body: Lítotes understates by negation: “no me disgusta” quietly means “I quite like it”. A doble sentido lets one utterance carry two readings at once, often for humour or tact — a phrase you can take innocently or knowingly. Reading both layers, and the tone that tips you off, is the essence of C2 comprehension.

ex.es: El plan no está mal del todo… tú sabrás.
ex.en: The plan isn't half bad… you know best.
—Did you like his speech? —It was… very long.

takeaways: Sarcasm/irony inverts the words; tone and context are the cues, not the vocabulary.
Connotation ≠ denotation: flaco/esquelético, curioso/cotilla, ahorrador/tacaño reveal attitude.
Implicatura: ‘Hace frío aquí’ can be a request (‘shut the window’), not a fact.
Lítotes understates by negation: ‘no está mal’ / ‘no me disgusta’ = genuine approval.

mistakes.w: Calling someone ‘tacaño’ when you mean to praise their careful budgeting.
mistakes.r: Use ‘ahorrador’ for praise; ‘tacaño’ is an insult.
mistakes.why: They share a denotation but opposite connotations — one flatters, one condemns.

mistakes.w: Answering ‘Hace frío aquí’ with only ‘Sí, un poco’ and doing nothing.
mistakes.r: Read the implicature and close the window (or offer to).
mistakes.why: Pragmatically it's often a polite request, not a comment on the temperature.

mistakes.w: Taking ‘No me disgusta’ as lukewarm or negative.
mistakes.r: Read it as lítotes: ‘I actually like it quite a lot’.
mistakes.why: Negating ‘disgustar’ understates genuine approval; it's warmer than it sounds.

exercises.prompt: Con tono seco, alguien dice: “¡Qué bien, otra reunión!” Significa que…
exercises.prompt_en: Deadpan, someone says “Oh great, another meeting!” It means…
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! El tono seco invierte el sentido → ironía.
exercises.no: The flat tone flips the literal words: it's ironic — he's fed up with meetings.

exercises.prompt: ¿Qué palabra elige quien quiere criticar a alguien por no gastar nunca?
exercises.prompt_en: Which word does someone pick to criticize a person for never spending?
exercises.no: For a negative judgment it's ‘tacaño’ (stingy); ‘ahorrador’ would praise the same behaviour.

exercises.prompt: Build: "It's not that I dislike it; quite the opposite."
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Lítotes: negar el disgusto para afirmar aprecio.
exercises.no: “No es que me disguste, sino todo lo contrario” — understatement (lítotes) that actually signals approval.

exercises.prompt: No es curioso, es un ___: se entera de la vida de todos.
exercises.prompt_en: He's not inquisitive, he's a nosy gossip: he knows everyone's business.
exercises.hint: The disparaging word for a nosy busybody.
exercises.no: The disparaging counterpart of ‘curioso’ is ‘cotilla’ (nosy gossip).

exercises.prompt: Match each utterance to what it really implies.
exercises.ok: ¡Excelente! Lees la intención, no solo las palabras.

exercises.tts: No es que me disguste, es que preferiría otra cosa.
accepted: no es que me disguste es que preferiria otra cosa
exercises.translation: It's not that I dislike it, it's that I'd prefer something else.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “No es que me disguste…” — lítotes cortés.
exercises.no: It was: “No es que me disguste, es que preferiría otra cosa.” (polite understatement).

exercises.scenario: Working late at a friend's place, and it's getting cold 🪟

lines.speaker: Elena
lines.en: Ugh, it's cold in here, don't you think?

options.text: Tienes razón, ahora mismo cierro la ventana.
Sí, en invierno siempre baja la temperatura.
Pues yo tengo bastante calor, la verdad.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Captaste la implicatura: era una petición.
exercises.no: It's an implicature — a polite request to close the window — so the natural reply is to offer to close it.

exercises.say: No es que me disguste, es todo lo contrario.
exercises.en: It's not that I dislike it — quite the opposite.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the rhythm of “No es que me disguste, es todo lo contrario.”

vocab.en: it's not bad (= it's actually good)
